You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:

 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   $v_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   Ripple $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$
    *   Current Best: `SSHI_FullBridge` (score 67.89)
        *   Passes 4/6 conditions.
        *   Fails S3 ripple (0.056 V vs 0.05 V) and S4 settled (0.031 V vs 0.02 V).
        *   It uses a synchronous switch for charge inversion (SSHI) and a full-bridge rectifier to the output.

    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` is very close.
    *   Failure on S4 `settled` (0.031 V) means the output voltage is still drifting at the end of the 0.8s window. This usually happens when the storage capacitor $C_1$ is too large (slow time constant) or the power delivered is just barely enough to maintain the voltage.
    *   Failure on S3 `ripple` (0.056 V) means $C_1$ is too small to buffer the energy pulses against the load $R_L$.
    *   This is a classic trade-off: $C_1$ needs to be larger to reduce ripple, but smaller to settle faster.

    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` is essentially a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) frontend followed by a rectifier.
    *   Wait, let's look at the components of `SSHI_FullBridge`:
        *   L1, S1, G1 (SSHI inversion)
        *   D1-D4 (Full-bridge rectifier)
        *   C1 (Storage)
        *   DZ1 (Zener clamp)
    *   If we can't find a perfect $C_1$ value to satisfy both ripple and settling time, we might need a way to decouple the energy pulse from the load or refine the rectification.

    *   Wait, look at the `SSHI_FullBridge` components:
        `D1 D pzp out DSCH`, `D2 D pzn out DSCH`, `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`, `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`
        This is a full-bridge rectifier.
        Wait, is this the most efficient way to extract energy from an SSHI-processed signal?
        SSHI usually works by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks. This increases the available voltage.
        The current design: $\text{Piezo} \to \text{SSHI} \to \text{Rectifier} \to C_{out}$.

    *   Let's re-evaluate the "S4 settled" failure. $dv = |mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)| = 0.031\text{ V}$.
        This means the capacitor is still charging/discharging significantly.
        If the load $R_L$ is $22\text{ k}\Omega$ (S4), and $V_{out} \approx 3.3\text{ V}$, the current is $3.3/22000 \approx 150\text{ }\mu\text{A}$.
        $C_1 = 3.66\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ is used in the best design.
        Time constant $\tau = R_L \cdot C_1 = 22\text{ k}\Omega \cdot 3.66\text{ }\mu\text{F} \approx 0.08\text{ s}$.
        The window is $0.1\text{ s}$. $dv$ is related to the difference in average voltages. If the system hasn't reached equilibrium, $dv$ will be high.

    *   To reduce ripple (S3), we need more capacitance.
    *   To reduce $dv$ (S4), we need less capacitance (to settle faster) or more power (to reach equilibrium faster).
    *   Since the power is already quite high (S4 $P_{load} = 0.494\text{ }\mu\text{W}$, while $V^2/R_L = 3.3^2/22000 = 0.495\text{ }\mu\text{W}$), we are exactly at the equilibrium point.
    *   The struggle is the time constant. If $C_1$ is too large, it takes too long to settle. If $C_1$ is too small, the ripple $v_{pp}$ is too high.

    *   Can we use a different rectification method?
    *   Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge or a different configuration? But full-bridge is generally best for AC.
    *   What if we add a second capacitor or a filter?
    *   Actually, the problem is that the `SSHI_FullBridge` is almost there. The "S4 settled" and "S3 ripple" are very small failures.
    *   Maybe adding a small series resistance to the output capacitor (not possible, $C$ is $out$ to $0$) or a slightly different topology.

    *   Let's think about the SSHI part. The current SSHI uses one inductor and one switch to flip the piezo voltage.
    *   What if we used a more advanced SSHI or a different energy extraction method?
    *   The "Repeated Problem" warning says: "too little power reaches the output... Change the part of the circuit responsible for it". But `SSHI_FullBridge` actually has plenty of power! It's failing on `ripple` and `settled`, not `vout_min`.

    *   Wait, let's look at the `S3 ripple` again: $0.056\text{ V}$. The limit is $0.05\text{ V}$.
    *   And `S4 settled`: $0.031\text{ V}$. The limit is $0.02\text{ V}$.
    *   These are very close. Maybe a slightly different capacitor arrangement or a better way to smooth the output?
    *   What if we use a capacitor divider or a small inductor in series with the storage capacitor (forming a LC filter)?
    *   `LC_Filtered_SSHI` was tried and failed miserably. Why? Because it had an inductor between the rectifier and the output capacitor: `L2 L mid out 0.001`. This likely caused huge voltage swings and slow startup.

    *   Wait, if we put a small inductor `L` and a capacitor `C` as a low-pass filter *after* the rectifier, it might reduce ripple without needing a massive `C` that slows down settling.
    *   Current `SSHI_FullBridge`: Rectifier $\to C_{out}$.
    *   Proposed: Rectifier $\to L_{filter} \to C_{out}$.
    *   Wait, the `LC_Filtered_SSHI` did exactly that. Let's look at why it failed.
        `L2 L mid out 0.001` (1 mH)
        `C1 C out 0 2.2uF`
        The output node `out` is where the load $R_L$ is.
        The rectifier outputs to `mid`.
        So we have a filter: `mid` $\to$ `L2` $\to$ `out`.
        This is a standard LC filter. Why did it fail?
        `S1 vavg = 2.04, vmax = 2.17, vpp = 259mV, tup = 0.657s`.
        The $v_{pp}$ is $259\text{ mV}$, which is huge! And it didn't settle.
        The issue might be the inductor value (1 mH might be too large) or the way it interacts with the switching.

    *   Let's try a different approach for the ripple/settle trade-off.
    *   What if we use a larger $C_{out}$ to fix ripple, but a way to speed up startup?
    *   Wait, the `SSHI_FullBridge` already has $t_{up} = 0.139\text{ s}$ to $0.244\text{ s}$, which is well within the $0.4\text{ s}$ limit.
    *   The only problem is $dv$ (settling) and $v_{pp}$ (ripple).
    *   If I increase $C_1$ to fix $v_{pp}$ (S3), $dv$ (S4) will get worse because the time constant $\tau = R_L C_1$ increases.
    *   If I decrease $C_1$ to fix $dv$ (S4), $v_{pp}$ (S3) will get worse.

    *   Is there a way to reduce ripple without increasing the DC time constant?
    *   A small inductor in series with the output is one way. But as we saw, the `LC_Filtered_SSHI` failed.
    *   Maybe the inductor was too large? 1 mH at 100 Hz?
    *   $X_L = 2 \pi f L = 2 \pi \cdot 100 \cdot 10^{-3} \approx 0.6\text{ }\Omega$. That's very small.
    *   Wait, the `LC_Filtered_SSHI` had:
        `L1 L pzp n1 0.0002` (SSHI)
        `L2 L mid out 0.001` (Filter)
        The `mid` node is the output of the full-bridge rectifier.
        The rectifier is `D1 pzp mid`, `D2 pzn mid`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn`.
        Wait, this rectifier is not a full bridge.
        A full bridge is:
        `D1 pzp out`, `D2 pzn out`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn`.
        No, that's not right.
        A standard full-bridge rectifier for a signal between $A$ and $B$ to a DC output $V_{out}$ and $GND$:
        - Diode 1: $A \to V_{out}$
        - Diode 2: $B \to V_{out}$
        - Diode 3: $GND \to A$
        - Diode 4: $GND \to B$
        This is exactly what `SSHI_FullBridge` has.
        Now look at `LC_Filtered_SSHI` again:
        `D1 pzp mid`, `D2 pzn mid`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn`.
        This is the same bridge, but the output is `mid`.
        Then `L2` is from `mid` to `out`.
        `C1` is from `out` to $0$.
        This is a $\Pi$-filter if there was a cap at `mid`, but here it's just an L-filter.
        The problem might be that the rectifier diodes $D_1, D_2$ are now switching into an inductor $L_2$. This can create huge spikes and affect the SSHI timing.

    *   Let's try to refine the `SSHI_FullBridge` by adding a very small capacitor in parallel with the rectifier output (at node `mid`) and then a small inductor before the final storage capacitor.
    *   No, that's too many components. Let's try to keep it simple.
    *   Is there another way to improve the `SSHI_FullBridge`?
    *   What if we change the rectifier to a different topology?
    *   Maybe a charge pump? No, too complex.
    *   What about a synchronous rectifier? We only have 2 SYNC controllers. One is already used for SSHI.

    *   Let's look at the $S_3$ ripple again. $S_3$ is "strong excitation, light load".
        $I_p = 40\text{ }\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 22\text{ k}\Omega$.
        $V_{out} \approx 3.3\text{ V}$.
        The ripple is $0.056\text{ V}$.
        If we just slightly increase $C_1$, the ripple will drop.
        The $S_4$ settled failure: $dv = 0.031\text{ V}$.
        $S_4$ is "weakest excitation".
        $I_p = 8\text{ }\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 22\text{ k}\Omega$.
        $V_{out} \approx 3.3\text{ V}$.
        The power delivered is $0.494\text{ }\mu\text{W}$, and the load needs $3.3^2 / 22000 = 0.495\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        The system is *barely* sustaining the voltage. This is why it takes so long to settle.
        If we can't increase the power, the only way to settle faster is to decrease $C_1$.
        But decreasing $C_1$ increases ripple on $S_3$.
